lead: A gear tooth fails in one of two places. The root cracks in bending fatigue, or the flank pits and wears. One material must resist both, and the two demands pull against each other: a hard surface tends to be brittle, while bending needs a tough core. Gear material choice is therefore a package of core strength, surface hardness and heat treatment, matched to load, speed and cost. It decides whether a Chennai water-plant gearbox lasts ten years or two.
prereq: You need: tensile strength and hardness of steels (selection of materials), and module and pitch diameter from gear nomenclature.

blocks.text: A tooth is a short cantilever. The root bending stress is carried by the whole section, so the core must be strong and tough; a hard, brittle core chips at the root under shock. The flank carries repeated rolling with sliding and fails by pitting and wear, which is a surface hardness problem.

Surface hardness is usually quoted as BHN, the Brinell hardness number: a 10 mm hardened ball is pressed in with 3000 kgf and the load is divided by the dent area, so BHN is in kgf/mm². Very hard cases are quoted in HRC (Rockwell C) or HV (Vickers): 58 HRC is about 600 BHN on the same scale. For steel the ultimate tensile strength is roughly 3.4 × BHN in MPa; that is an estimate from a hardness test, not a design value. Many Indian textbooks take the allowable bending stress of a gear tooth as σb = σut/3, and the wear of a steel pair through the load-stress factor K = 0.16(BHN/100)² N/mm²; both are used in spur gear design.

The pinion rule matters more than any single number. When a 20-tooth pinion drives a 60-tooth gear, the pinion turns three times for each turn of the gear, so each pinion tooth is loaded three times as often. Fatigue damage grows with the number of cycles, so with equal hardness the pinion pits first. For through-hardened pairs make the pinion about 30 to 50 BHN harder than the gear, so both reach the end of their life together. A case-hardened pinion is usually far harder than its gear anyway.

Plain carbon steels with 0.3 to 0.6 % carbon (C40, C45, 40C8) are the shop-floor default. C45 normalised is about 200 to 230 BHN; hardened and tempered it reaches 250 to 300 BHN. It is cheap and machines freely. Above about 350 BHN a through-hardened gear is hard to cut and distorts, so harder surfaces come from case treatments instead. Alloy steels add chromium for hardenability, nickel for core toughness and molybdenum against temper brittleness; through-hardened 40Cr1 or 42CrMo4 keeps 300 to 350 BHN in sections too thick for plain carbon steel.

items: Case carburising: a low-carbon alloy steel (0.15 to 0.25 % C, for example 20MnCr5) is held at about 900 to 930 °C in a carbon-rich gas, so carbon diffuses 0.8 to 1.5 mm into the surface; the gear is then quenched and tempered. Surface 58 to 62 HRC, core 30 to 40 HRC. Chosen for heavy load, shock and high speed, as in vehicle gearboxes.

Nitriding: ammonia gas at about 500 to 550 °C for many hours, with no quench. The case is thin, 0.3 to 0.6 mm, and very hard, roughly 600 to 1000 HV depending on the steel. Distortion is very small, so it suits internal gears and large rings that cannot be ground after hardening.
Induction or flame hardening: the flanks are heated quickly and quenched at once, giving about 50 to 55 HRC over a tough core. Used on large-module gears made of medium-carbon steel.

blocks.text: Distortion is the hidden cost of hardening. A carburised gear must be ground after hardening, so the drawing leaves grinding stock on each flank and says 'grind after hardening'.

Grey cast iron (FG 200, FG 260; the number is the minimum tensile strength in MPa) has flake graphite that damps vibration and breaks chips. It is cheap and quiet but weak in tension and shock. Use it for large, slow gears, usually running with a steel pinion; never for a small high-speed pinion.

Bronze belongs to worm wheels. A worm drive slides rather than rolls, so the wheel must be conformable, resist seizure and have low friction against steel. The standard pair is a phosphor bronze wheel with a hardened, ground steel worm; the bronze is always the softer member.

items: Nylon and acetal gears run quietly with little lubrication and absorb shock, but they creep, swell with moisture and get rid of heat badly, so keep load and speed low (food mixers, printers).
Phenolic laminates and sintered powder-metal gears serve quiet timing drives and cheap, mass-produced small gears.

examples.question: A 7.5 kW motor at 1440 rpm drives a 20-tooth pinion of module 3 mm through a 1:3 pair with moderate shock. Find the pitch line velocity, the torque and the tangential load, and recommend a material pair.
steps: Pitch diameter: d<sub>1</sub> = m z<sub>1</sub> = 3 × 20 = 60 mm = 0.060 m.
Pitch line velocity: v = πd<sub>1n</sub>/60 = π × 0.060 × 1440/60 = 4.52 m/s.
Tangential load: F<sub>t</sub> = 2T/d<sub>1</sub> = 2 × 49.74/0.060 = 1658 N. Check: P/v = 7500/4.524 = 1658 N.

Choice: the speed is moderate and the shock is moderate, so a through-hardened steel pair is enough: a C45 pinion at about 300 BHN with a C45 gear at about 250 BHN (50 BHN softer, because the pinion sees three times the cycles). If the box must be smaller or the shock grows, change to a case-carburised 20MnCr5 pinion.
examples.answer: v = 4.52 m/s, T = 49.74 N·m, F<sub>t</sub> = 1.66 kN; a through-hardened C45 pair, pinion about 300 BHN and gear about 250 BHN.

examples.question: A 40C8 steel pinion (σ<sub>ut</sub> = 600 N/mm²) runs with a gear of the same steel. Both are hardened to 300 BHN. Find the allowable bending stress, the load-stress factor K, and how much the wear capacity rises if the surfaces are hardened to 380 BHN instead. The pinion has 20 teeth, runs at 1440 rpm with ratio 3, for 10 000 h: find the cycles on a pinion tooth and on a gear tooth.
steps: Allowable bending stress: σ<sub>b</sub> = σ<sub>ut</sub>/3 = 600/3 = 200 N/mm².
Load-stress factor at 300 BHN: K = 0.16(300/100)² = 0.16 × 9 = 1.44 N/mm².
At 380 BHN: K = 0.16 × 3.8² = 0.16 × 14.44 = 2.31 N/mm². The wear load is proportional to K, so the wear capacity rises by 2.31/1.44 = 1.60 times, that is 60 %, with the same size of gear.
Gear speed = 1440/3 = 480 rpm, so gear cycles = 60 × 480 × 10 000 = 2.88 × 10⁸, a third of the pinion's.
examples.answer: σ<sub>b</sub> = 200 N/mm²; K = 1.44 N/mm² at 300 BHN and 2.31 N/mm² at 380 BHN (60 % more wear capacity); 8.64 × 10⁸ pinion cycles against 2.88 × 10⁸ gear cycles.

traps: Choosing the hardest steel for both wheels. A hard case needs a tough core; a tooth hardened right through is brittle and chips at the root under shock.
Reading BHN as a strength in MPa. 300 BHN suggests about 1000 MPa tensile strength for steel, but only as an estimate, and the allowable bending stress is a fraction of the strength.
Mixing hardness scales: 58 HRC is about 600 BHN. Compare pinion and gear hardness on one scale.
Pairing bronze with bronze in a worm drive, or a soft worm with a hard wheel. The wheel is the bronze member and the worm is hardened and ground.
Using cast iron for a small high-speed pinion because it runs quietly. Damping does not make up for its low tensile and shock strength.

quiz.q: Define BHN and give its unit.
quiz.a: Brinell hardness number: the load of a 10 mm ball pressed in with 3000 kgf divided by the dent area. Unit kgf/mm².

quiz.q: State the usual hardness difference between a through-hardened pinion and its gear, and why.
quiz.a: The pinion is about 30 to 50 BHN harder, because each pinion tooth is loaded ratio-times more often; this evens out the fatigue lives.

quiz.q: Why is a case-hardened tooth better than a tooth hardened right through, under shock?
quiz.a: The through-hardened tooth is brittle everywhere, so the root cracks under shock. Case hardening gives a hard flank for wear and keeps a tough core for bending.

quiz.q: A 3 kW, 960 rpm motor drives a 25-tooth pinion of module 2.5 mm. Find the pitch line velocity and the tangential load.
Find K for a steel pair hardened to 350 BHN, and the allowable bending stress for σ<sub>ut</sub> = 720 N/mm².
A 300 BHN pinion meshes with a 300 BHN gear at 4:1. Predict the failure and give the fix.
quiz.a: Each pinion tooth is loaded four times as often, so at equal hardness the pinion pits first. Make the pinion harder, about 340 to 350 BHN, or case-harden it, so the two lives match.

quiz.q: Why does nitriding suit an internal gear ring?
quiz.a: Nitriding needs no quench, so the ring hardly distorts and needs no grinding afterwards; internal teeth are hard to grind.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gear heat treatment is moving to low-pressure vacuum carburising with gas quenching, which cuts distortion and the grinding after it. Controlled shot peening of the root fillet raises bending fatigue life and is standard in vehicle gearboxes. Search for vacuum carburising, shot peening of gear roots and clean gear steel.
